title: Migration since the Brexit vote: what's changed in six charts
meta_description: ONS migration statistics for the first full year since the UK voted to leave the EU. These figures refer to people arriving or leaving the UK for 12 months or more. What's changed in six charts?

breadcrumb.text: Migration since the Brexit vote: what's changed in six charts

lede: With a full year of migration statistics since the UK voted to leave the EU, what do we know so far?

body.text: 30 November 2017
We now have migration statistics for the first full year since the UK voted to leave the EU. These figures refer to people arriving or leaving the UK for 12 months or more.
Here’s what we know so far.

body.h3: There’s been a fall in net migration, after a recent peak
body.text: There’s been a fall in net migration, after a recent peak

body.h3: There’s been a fall in net migration, after a recent peak
body.text: In the year to June 2017, there were 230,000 more people coming to live in the UK than leaving the UK to live abroad – this is “net migration”. When net migration is above zero, as it has been continually since 1994, migration is adding to the UK population.

body.h3: There’s been a fall in net migration, after a recent peak
body.text: Net migration is 106,000 lower than it was the year before: this is the largest fall in any 12-month period since records began in 1964 and represents a reduction of around a third. But it’s important to note that this fall was from a very high net migration figure of 336,000 in the year to June 2016.

body.h3: There’s been a fall in net migration, after a recent peak
body.text: Net migration had been increasing since 2012; the recent fall sees net migration returning to the level we saw in 2014. This level of net migration is not unusual as we have seen net migration vary between 140,000 and 336,000 over the last 20 years.

body.h3: Most of the fall in net migration is because of EU citizens
body.text: Most of the fall in net migration is because of EU citizens

body.h3: Most of the fall in net migration is because of EU citizens
body.text: Over three-quarters of the fall in net migration was due to EU citizens. But more EU citizens are still coming to the UK than leaving, showing EU net migration is adding to the UK population.

body.h3: Most of the fall in net migration is because of EU citizens
body.text: The largest falls were from citizens of western EU countries (the EU15 group, for example France, Germany and Spain) and central and eastern Europe countries (the EU8 group, for example Poland).

body.h3: Most of the fall in net migration is because of EU citizens
body.text: Some of this change might be because of economic changes across the EU, for example improved job opportunities and the fall in the value of the pound.

body.h3: Most of the fall in net migration is because of EU citizens
body.text: Meanwhile, there’s been a small decrease in net migration of non-EU citizens and net migration of British citizens hasn’t changed – more British people still leave the UK than come or return to live here from abroad.

body.h3: Fewer people are coming to live in the UK…
body.text: Fewer people are coming to live in the UK…

body.h3: Fewer people are coming to live in the UK…
body.text: 572,000 people came to live in the UK in the year to June 2017: that’s 80,000 fewer people than in the previous year.

body.h3: Fewer people are coming to live in the UK…
body.text: This reduction is high, but it’s from a starting point of 652,000 in the year to June 2016, which was the highest figure on record.

body.h3: Fewer people are coming to live in the UK…
body.text: It was driven by falls both in the numbers of EU citizens (down 19% on the previous year) as well as non-EU citizens (down 10%) coming to the UK.

body.h3: …and more EU citizens are leaving
body.text: …and more EU citizens are leaving

body.h3: …and more EU citizens are leaving
body.text: The largest change in the number of people leaving the UK was from EU citizens, increasing by 29% to 123,000.

body.h3: …and more EU citizens are leaving
body.text: Of these EU citizens leaving the UK, 43,000 said that their main reason for leaving the UK was to return home, rather than because of work or for other reasons. This is an increase of 54% from the previous year. Recently the number of EU citizens leaving the UK has almost reached the higher level seen during the 2008 recession.

body.h3: …and more EU citizens are leaving
body.text: The number of British and non-EU citizens leaving the UK has remained stable over the past year.

body.h3: Fewer EU citizens are coming to the UK to look for work
body.text: Fewer EU citizens are coming to the UK to look for work

body.h3: Fewer EU citizens are coming to the UK to look for work
body.text: Of the EU citizens coming to the UK for work reasons, a greater percentage were likely to have a definite job than those arriving in previous years.

body.h3: Fewer EU citizens are coming to the UK to look for work
body.text: The number coming to look for work has more than halved in the year to June 2017, while the number of EU citizens arriving for a definite job has remained similar.

body.h3: Fewer EU citizens are coming to the UK to look for work
body.text: The majority of the decrease in EU citizens looking for work was due to western EU citizens (the EU15 group) and central and eastern Europe citizens (the EU8).

body.h3: Fewer EU citizens are coming to the UK to look for work
body.h4: EU citizens coming to the UK for work reasons, years ending December 2007 to June 2017
body.text: Overseas nationals require a National Insurance number to work or claim benefits in the UK. The number of EU nationals registering for a National Insurance number over the last year has decreased by 13%, showing a similar recent pattern to the migration statistics.

body.h3: Fewer EU citizens are coming to the UK to look for work
body.h4: EU citizens coming to the UK for work reasons, years ending December 2007 to June 2017
body.text: Despite these decreases, EU net migration is still positive (as it has been since the 1990s), so you may expect the number of EU nationals employed in the UK to continue to rise. In July to September 2017, there were 2.38 million EU nationals employed in the UK, up 112,000 on the same period the previous year.

body.h3: More EU citizens are applying to become British citizens
body.text: More EU citizens are applying to become British citizens

body.h3: More EU citizens are applying to become British citizens
body.text: In the year to June 2017, nearly 28,500 EU nationals applied to become British citizens, up 80% compared with the previous year. EU nationals need to be living in the UK for a minimum period before they can be granted UK citizenship, so are likely to have been longer-term residents rather than recent arrivals.

body.h3: More EU citizens are applying to become British citizens
body.text: Applications from non-EU nationals to become British citizens have fallen by 44% since 2010, probably because of the recent reduction in non-EU nationals settling in the UK as well as changes to eligibility.

body.h3: More EU citizens are applying to become British citizens
body.h4: Applications for British citizenship by nationality, years ending June 2008 to June 2017
body.text: In the year to June 2017, the Home Office issued a record number (145,400) of permanent residence documents and cards to people from the European Economic Area (EEA) and their families1. This was more than five times the figure for the previous year (27,200).

body.h3: More EU citizens are applying to become British citizens
body.h4: Applications for British citizenship by nationality, years ending June 2008 to June 2017
body.text: This is likely to be because of more people wanting to obtain confirmation of their rights following the referendum result; there were also some rule changes in the second half of 2015.
